clue.text: Support advertiser circulating source of unsolicited advice

parts.note: to back someone is to support them

indicators.note: something circulating moves round and round, so the letters of the word before it get stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder for the rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone promoting a product goes round handing out advice nobody asked for.
explanation.definitionFit: A backseat driver is a passenger who keeps telling the person at the wheel how to drive, hence anyone offering unwanted guidance.

clue.text: Swine, big noise, doctor and idiot get authorisation to fly

parts.note: a boar is a male pig
a din is a loud racket
GP, general practitioner, is a family doctor
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A motley list of a pig, a racket, a medic and a fool all being cleared for a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big noise' looks like an important person, but here it is simply a loud noise. GP is the British term for a family doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A boarding pass is the document an airline issues allowing a passenger onto the plane.

clue.text: Supply feline to queen

parts.note: a cat is a feline
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword queen

explanation.surface: Someone hands a cat over to the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: To cater is to provide food or whatever is needed, so it is a synonym of supply as a verb.

clue.text: Wise man suppressing constant anger and profanity

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold something down within, so the wise man keeps the next pieces inside him

parts.note: a sage is a wise person
c is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light
to rile is to anger

explanation.surface: A sage keeps his temper in check and avoids swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constant' is a lone letter here, the symbol scientists use for a fixed quantity such as the speed of light, and it goes in along with the anger.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacrilege is the violation of something sacred, and profanity in its older sense means irreverence toward holy things.

clue.text: A Liberal member journalist accused without proof

parts.note: taken as written
L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal
a leg is a limb, a member of the body
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A Liberal MP and a reporter are both charged on flimsy grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a member of parliament, but here it is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: An alleged crime or offender has been claimed or asserted but not yet established as fact.

clue.text: Constructs 500 flexible sieves

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500

indicators.note: something flexible can be bent into a new shape, so the following word is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder for the rearrangement

explanation.surface: A manufacturer builds five hundred bendy strainers.
explanation.definitionFit: To devise is to invent or plan something out, so it matches constructs as a verb in the third person.

clue.text: Bury short trainee

indicators.note: short means cut off before its end, so the last letter of the word that follows is dropped

parts.note: an intern is a trainee on a work placement

explanation.surface: An instruction to bury a trainee who is not very tall.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to place a dead body in a grave, which is exactly what bury means.

clue.text: Repeat run redesigned to thrill

indicators.note: redesigned means given a new layout, so the words before it are laid out in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: A rerun of a show is reworked to excite viewers.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrapture is to fill someone with delight, much like thrilling them.

clue.text: Exploit vacuous American jerk

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of its inside and only its outer pair remains

parts.note: only the first and last letters of the word stay
a tic is an involuntary twitch or jerk

explanation.surface: Someone takes advantage of an empty-headed American idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' in the surface is an insult; in the wordplay it is a twitch. 'Exploit' reads as a verb but is the noun, a daring deed.
explanation.definitionFit: An antic is a playful or absurd act, a caper, and an exploit is a notable deed or escapade.

clue.text: Can the French tax Circle Line?

parts.note: la is French for the, in its feminine form
VAT is value added tax
the letter O is round like a circle
RY is an abbreviation for railway, a rail line

explanation.surface: A question about whether the French could charge a levy on London's Circle Line.
explanation.walkthrough: The Circle Line is a London Underground route, but here the words are split. 'Can' is not the verb but slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Can is American slang for a toilet, and a lavatory is a toilet or the room containing one.

clue.text: Bank to hold fast to smaller amount without mercy

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so the first word wraps round the following pieces

parts.note: to bank on someone is to rely on them
Lent is the Christian season of fasting
less means a smaller amount

explanation.surface: A bank keeps a tight grip on its shrinking funds and shows no pity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' is not speed but abstaining from food, the sense in which Lent is a fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Relentlessly means persistently and harshly, never easing off, which is acting without mercy.

clue.text: Sweetheart venturing around lake

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the first word wraps itself round the second

parts.note: daring means venturing boldly
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A lover goes out on an adventure round a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Darling and sweetheart are both affectionate terms for a beloved person.

clue.text: Small wrinkle (not medium) causes moral difficulty

indicators.note: not medium says the letter standing for medium is taken out of the word before it

parts.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
to crumple is to crease or wrinkle

explanation.surface: A tiny crease in a garment becomes an ethical dilemma.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the size label for medium; removing it from CRUMPLE and adding S gives SCRUPLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A scruple is a feeling of doubt about whether an action is right, an ethical qualm.

clue.text: Jog naked, covering genitals initially

indicators.note: covering means wrapping round, so the first word goes outside the chosen letter

parts.note: nude means naked

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A naturist runner preserves a little modesty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jog' looks like running but means a small push.
explanation.definitionFit: To jog someone is to give them a light push, the same as a nudge, as in jogging an elbow.

clue.text: Confinement of Parisian number one trapped by heavy weight

parts.note: de is French for of, as a Parisian would say it
ten is a number

indicators.note: something trapped by another is held inside it, so the single letter goes within the weight

parts.note: a ton is a large unit of weight
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A French champion is pinned down by a heavyweight opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of Parisian' together means the French for of, so 'of' does double work in the reading; I sits inside TON.
explanation.definitionFit: Detention is the state of being held in custody or kept in, which is a form of confinement.

clue.text: Oldest IT utensil's content is poor

indicators.note: the content of something is what sits inside it, so the answer lies within the run of words

parts.note: the letters run across the words, skipping the opening O and closing NSIL'S

explanation.surface: Even the most ancient computer gadget is rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' looks like a feeling of satisfaction but means what is contained.
explanation.definitionFit: Destitute means lacking money and basic necessities, an extreme degree of being poor.

clue.text: Disparages that cockney bloke with fruit

indicators.note: Cockneys famously drop an initial H, so the word for that bloke loses its first letter

parts.note: him is the pronoun for a man, that bloke
peaches are fruit

explanation.surface: A London market trader runs down his rival's produce.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class East London accent, which drops H sounds: HIM becomes 'IM.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach a person's character or testimony is to call it into question and discredit it, which is to disparage it.

clue.text: Wizard dines regularly on special plants in Staffordshire

parts.note: Harry Potter is the boy wizard of the novels

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word before it is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the word
S is an abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: A wizard eats a regular meal of magical vegetation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plants' sounds botanical but means factories. The Potteries is the area around Stoke-on-Trent in Staffordshire, England, historically the home of pottery making.
explanation.definitionFit: The Potteries is the name for the Staffordshire towns famous for their ceramic works, the factories implied by plants.

clue.text: Fashionable dress includes bit of ribbing digging into flesh

parts.note: in means fashionable

indicators.note: includes means takes inside, so the dress holds the single letter

parts.note: a gown is a dress

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is just its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A trendy ribbed frock cuts uncomfortably into the wearer's skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ribbing' suggests the ridged texture of the dress, but only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingrown describes something, typically a toenail or hair, that has grown into the surrounding flesh.

clue.text: Dreadful sound coming from disorganised creches

indicators.note: disorganised means put in no proper order, so the letters of the word after it are muddled

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: A terrible racket rises from chaotic nurseries.
explanation.walkthrough: A creche is a nursery where small children are looked after.
explanation.definitionFit: A screech is a harsh, piercing cry, the kind of noise that grates on the ear.

clue.text: Request time to fold

parts.note: a plea is an appeal or request
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a little time before giving up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fold' in the surface suggests giving up, as in a card game; here it is a crease in cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleat is a doubled-over fold pressed or stitched into fabric.

clue.text: Misbehave with alcohol, golf and chanting

parts.note: to sin is to do wrong
gin is an alcoholic spirit
Golf is the NATO alphabet word for G

explanation.surface: A rowdy day out of drinking, golf and football-style chants.
explanation.definitionFit: Chanting is singing or intoning words, often repetitively, so the two are near synonyms.

clue.text: Nationality of independent artist on quiz show

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for independent
RA, Royal Academician, is a crossword artist
QI is a British TV comedy quiz show

explanation.surface: Asking where a freelance painter appearing on a TV quiz comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: QI is a long-running BBC panel quiz hosted by Stephen Fry and later Sandi Toksvig; 'on' places it after the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Iraqi names a person's nationality, someone from Iraq, so it answers what nationality is asked for.

clue.text: Fetch twig

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bring in a sum when sold, as an item fetches a price
second meaning: grasp or understand, in informal British usage

explanation.walkthrough: The pair suggests a dog fetching a stick, but both words are verbs with other senses: to twig is British slang for to understand.
explanation.definitionFit: To realise a price means to fetch it at sale, and to realise a truth means to understand or twig it.

clue.text: Starts to install galvanised layer over our home

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters, taken from each word that follows

parts.note: first letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A builder begins fitting a coat of galvanised metal over the house.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is a dome-shaped dwelling built from blocks of snow, a traditional Inuit home.

clue.text: Stick a warning in item of clothing

parts.note: to pin is to stick or fasten
taken as written
fore is the golfer's shouted warning

explanation.surface: Someone fastens a caution notice onto a garment.
explanation.walkthrough: A pinafore is a sleeveless apron-like dress worn over other clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinafore is a garment, a collarless apron or sleeveless dress, so it is an item of clothing.

clue.text: Student accommodation holds over two learners

indicators.note: over here means placed round, so the first word sits outside the pair of letters

parts.note: to have is to hold
L, for learner, twice, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: A university residence takes in a pair of new students.
explanation.walkthrough: Halls, short for halls of residence, is the British term for university dormitories.
explanation.definitionFit: Halls of residence are the buildings where university students live, usually shortened to halls.

clue.text: A tale about thin ice cracking is no longer relevant

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something cracking breaks apart, so the words before it are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: the words as printed, but the parse needs a second N they do not supply: the setter's slip
a story is a tale

explanation.surface: A story about breaking ice turns out to be stale news.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is A, then the rearranged letters, then STORY, but THIN ICE has one N too few: the answer needs an anagram of THINNICE, so the setter has slipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient history is an idiom for something that happened long ago and no longer matters.
